I've attached Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents (first half 2013) data for 33 London boroughs and a list showing which boroughs are geographic neighbors of each other.

Question: You can use a statistical method such as Getis-Ord Gi*, or any other method you choose, to identify boroughs where there is an unusually intense CONCENTRATION of high Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents (first half 2013) (a HOT spot) or low Recorded Crime per 10,000 residents (first half 2013) (a COLD spot), considering each borough TOGETHER WITH its neighbors as one combined local area.

This is different from asking whether a borough simply resembles its immediate neighbors -- instead, you are testing whether the COMBINED total (the borough together with its neighbors) is unusually large or small compared to the citywide average, regardless of how similar the borough is to any one neighbor individually.

Note: a borough whose own value is missing should not itself be reported as a hot or cold spot in your final answer. Note: dedicated spatial-statistics packages (pysal, esda, libpysal, geopandas, or similar) are NOT installed in this environment -- don't spend turns trying different import paths for them. Implement your chosen method directly using only pandas and numpy. If your method produces a z-score, use the standard critical values: |z| > 1.96 for 95% confidence, |z| > 2.576 for 99% confidence.

End your response with exactly one line listing every borough you identified, using HOT for hot spot and COLD for cold spot, and including the computed real number (e.g. a z-score) for each:

Thought: Load the crime‐rate dataset and the adjacency list, build for every borough the set consisting of itself plus all listed neighbours, compute for each borough the sum of crime-rate values over that whole local set, then derive z-scores for those sums across London. Flag boroughs with |z|>1.96 as HOT (positive z) or COLD (negative z). Finally, list those boroughs that meet the criterion.

Action:
```python
import pandas as pd, numpy as np, os, json, math, textwrap, itertools, re, typing, collections, random, statistics, datetime, functools, decimal, fractions, pprint, copy, decimal, bisect
# Load datasets
DATASET_PATH = "chunks_csv/getisord/getisord_crime_first_half_2013.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(DATASET_PATH)
adj = pd.read_csv("chunks_csv/borough_adjacency.csv")  # ADJACENCY_PATH variable isn't available in this environment.

# Build adjacency dictionary
neigh_dict = {b: set() for b in df['borough']}
for _, row in adj.iterrows():
    neigh_dict.setdefault(row['borough'], set()).add(row['neighbor'])
    neigh_dict.setdefault(row['neighbor'], set()).add(row['borough'])  # Ensure symmetry

# Compute local sums
local_sums = []
for b, val in df.set_index('borough')['crime_rate_value'].items():
    if pd.isna(val):
        continue
    local_set = {b}.union(neigh_dict.get(b, set()))
    values = df.set_index('borough').loc[list(local_set), 'crime_rate_value']
    local_sum = values.sum(skipna=True)
    local_sums.append((b, local_sum))

# Convert to DataFrame
local_df = pd.DataFrame(local_sums, columns=['borough', 'local_sum'])

# z-scores
mean = local_df['local_sum'].mean()
std = local_df['local_sum'].std(ddof=0)
local_df['z'] = (local_df['local_sum'] - mean) / std

# Identify hotspots/coldspots
hot_cold = local_df[local_df['z'].abs() > 1.96]
print(hot_cold.sort_values('z', ascending=False).to_string(index=False))
```
